text: The Kulungugu bomb attack was a failed assassination attempt on Kwame Nkrumah, the President of Ghana. On 1 August 1962, Nkrumah stopped in Kulungugu, a minor port of entry in the Pusiga District of Upper East Bawku. He was returning from a meeting with President Maurice Yaméogo in Tenkodogo, then known as Upper Volta, where they had signed documents related to the construction of the major hydroelectric project that would become Lake Volta. During the return journey, heavy rains caused difficulties for the Presidential convoy due to the country's poor roads. The convoy stopped at the outskirts of Bawku to greet school children who had been waving and catching glimpses of the President. A school child, Elizabeth Asantewaa, approached the President with a bouquet of flowers and was severely injured when the bomb exploded. The President was saved by his bodyguard, Captain Samuel Buckman, who instinctively wrestled him to the ground after hearing the ticking of the timing device. Both Nkrumah and Buckman sustained non-life-threatening injuries, but 55 other people were injured. Nkrumah was treated by a British doctor at Bawku Hospital, who removed shrapnel from his back and side. A memorial stands at the site of the bombing. Nkrumah accused Tawia Adamafio, the Minister of Information, Broadcasting and Presidential Affairs, Ako Adjei, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and H.H. Cofie-Crabbe, the Executive Secretary of the Convention People's Party, of being behind the assassination plot. The three were jailed under the Preventive Detention Act. A court headed by Chief Justice Arku Korsah cleared them after a one-year trial. Nkrumah dismissed Korsah and appointed a new court to re-trial the men. Nkrumah handpicked the jury that found the three guilty, and they were sentenced to death; later, the death sentences were commuted to twenty-year sentences. After Nkrumah was ousted from office in 1966, the National Liberation Council (NLC) released the three.
